title: Crusades and the Medieval Church
welcome_lead: Follow the call of Pope Urban II from Clermont 1095 to the fall of Acre 1291.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on the Crusades, papal authority and medieval Christendom.
final_note: You have weighed faith, plunder and politics across the eastern Mediterranean.

concepts.def: Expedition launched after Urban II's 1095 sermon at Clermont, capturing Jerusalem in July 1099.
Latin polities founded in the Levant after 1099, including the Kingdom of Jerusalem and County of Tripoli.
Sultan of Egypt and Syria who recaptured Jerusalem at the Battle of Hattin in 1187.
1189-92 campaign led by Richard I, Philip II and Frederick Barbarossa, securing a truce with Saladin.
Twelfth- and thirteenth-century papacy claiming supreme authority over Christendom, exemplified by Innocent III.
Remission of temporal punishment for sin, granted by the Church to crusaders and later sold widely.

walkthroughs.h2: Why did Christians answer Urban II's call?
walkthroughs.body_html: By 1095 Byzantine Emperor Alexios I requested western aid against Seljuk Turks. Urban II preached at Clermont offering remission of sins for those who recovered Jerusalem. Religious devotion, papal authority, knightly violence channelled into holy war, and the prospect of land combined to mobilise tens of thousands. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in July 1099 amid notorious massacres.

Saladin united Egypt and Syria and exploited crusader divisions. At Hattin in July 1187 he destroyed the Latin army and seized the True Cross; Jerusalem fell in October. The shock triggered the Third Crusade (1189-92). Richard I retook Acre but a negotiated truce in 1192 left Jerusalem in Muslim hands while securing pilgrim access.

walkthroughs.h2: Was the Church a unifying force?
walkthroughs.body_html: Traditional accounts emphasise the papacy under Innocent III (1198-1216) as the apex of medieval Christendom, calling crusades and convening the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215. Revisionists stress dissent: heresies, the sack of Constantinople in 1204 and clerical wealth fuelled critiques that anticipated later reform movements.
